abstract.p: Digital economy development changes manufacturing production and its energy requirements, but the carbon implications may differ across cities. This study examined nine mainland cities in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area over 2011–2024 using fixed-effects models, a spatial Durbin model (SDM), mediation regressions, and descriptive decoupling analysis. The reported SDM coefficient for digital economy development was negative ($-$0.3423, standard error 0.1631), whereas the decomposed average direct and total effects were statistically insignificant. In the non-spatial mediation model, the indirect association through the secondary-industry share represented 29.82% of the estimated total association, while the research and development (R&D) expenditure pathway was not statistically significant. The spatial indirect effect was also insignificant. Subgroup coefficients were negative in Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Foshan, and Dongguan ($-$0.9511) and positive but insignificant in the five peripheral cities (0.3047). These patterns suggest that digital development and manufacturing emissions have context-dependent relationships. They support evaluating digital investment alongside industrial composition and regional carbon accounting. The findings concern conditional associations in a small regional panel and a direct fuel-combustion inventory; they should be interpreted within those statistical and accounting boundaries.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Manufacturing regions face a difficult adjustment: they must sustain production and employment while reducing the carbon intensity and, ultimately, the absolute emissions of industrial activity. Digital technologies change the information available to firms, the organization of production, and the coordination of supply chains. Their environmental consequences depend on the activities they replace, the electricity they require, and the production expansion they make possible. A useful assessment therefore needs to distinguish emissions levels, emissions intensity, and broader measures of carbon efficiency.

Evidence from Chinese cities links digital development to carbon emission performance [1], while Ma et al. [2] examined whether research and development (R&D) investment moderates this relationship. These are related questions, but they concern different outcomes and mechanisms. Evidence on structural deviation [3] and industrial carbon efficiency [4] further suggests that industrial composition matters alongside production technology. Dynamic city-level analysis [5] and research on three major urban agglomerations [6] motivate closer attention to development stages and regional context. These studies provide a basis for examining manufacturing emissions within the Pearl River Delta (PRD) rather than assuming that national estimates apply uniformly to its constituent cities.

The present study concerns the nine mainland cities of the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area. Hong Kong and Macao form part of the regional setting but are outside the estimation sample. The nine cities share production networks and provincial institutions, while differing in manufacturing scale, specialization, and digital development. This setting allows a focused comparison within an integrated manufacturing region, although the small number of cities limits statistical precision and the scope for generalization.

Research on digital investment and carbon efficiency [7], emissions along the digital economy’s industry chain [8], and the interaction between energy structure and digitalization [9] illustrates why a single environmental interpretation is insufficient. Digital investment can influence production efficiency while also generating upstream energy demand. Information and communication technology (ICT) research outside China likewise considers transmission channels and country conditions [10]; earlier evidence on electricity consumption documents the energy demands associated with ICT expansion [11]. The Chinese digital economy also encompasses institutional and structural changes beyond the adoption of individual technologies [12]. Consequently, an aggregate city index should be interpreted as a measure of the wider digital environment rather than a direct measure of factory-level digital adoption.

Manufacturing-specific evidence on digital transformation and carbon competitiveness [13] helps narrow the sectoral question. Research on technological diversification and industrial carbon efficiency [14], together with provincial evidence on digital development and emissions intensity [15], shows the relevance of separating technology, composition, and scale. The present analysis follows that distinction. Its dependent variable is estimated direct fuel-combustion

Three questions guide the analysis. First, is digital economy development negatively associated with manufacturing fuel-combustion emissions after accounting for city effects, year effects, and observed covariates? Second, are industrial composition and R&D expenditure statistically consistent with the proposed channels? Third, do spatial impacts and subgroup estimates reveal a common regional pattern or contrasting relationships across core and peripheral cities?

A panel covering 2011–2024 was examined using fixed-effects and spatial models, separate mediation regressions, and descriptive decoupling analysis. The study examines whether the association between digital development and manufacturing emissions differs across cities within an integrated regional economy. It considers industrial composition and R&D expenditure as separate potential channels and compares local and cross-city associations using a spatial framework. Section 2 develops the analytical framework. Section 3 presents the data and methods. Section 4 reports results, Section 5 discusses their interpretation and policy implications, and Section 6 concludes.

sec.title: 2.1. Scale, composition, and technology
sec.p: Environmental economics distinguishes changes in production scale, economic composition, and production techniques. The trade–environment framework of Copeland and Taylor [16] and the growth analysis of Grossman and Krueger [17] provide foundations for this distinction. Applied to digital development, the scale channel concerns additional production; the composition channel concerns shifts among activities; and the technique channel concerns the emissions required to produce a given output. These channels can operate simultaneously and in opposing directions.

Directed technical change adds a further qualification: innovation responds to incentives and need not automatically favour cleaner technologies [18]. Digital applications may improve monitoring and equipment operation, but they can also support more production in emissions-intensive activities. Accordingly, the empirical hypothesis concerns the net conditional association in the sample, rather than a universal technological rule.
H1. Digital economy development is negatively associated with manufacturing carbon emissions, conditional on the specified city characteristics and fixed effects.

sec.title: 2.2. Industrial restructuring
sec.p: Digital connectivity can reduce coordination costs between suppliers and customers, making it easier to organize production across locations. It may also accompany the expansion of information services, design, and other activities that change the composition of city output. The literature on structural deviation [3] and manufacturing carbon efficiency [4] provides relevant empirical context, but neither broad structural adjustment nor a larger service sector necessarily means that existing manufacturing plants have become cleaner.

This study measures industrial structure (IND) using secondary-industry value added as a percentage of GDP. A decline in this share could arise through service-sector growth, a contraction of secondary industry, or changes in relative prices. Secondary industry also includes activities beyond manufacturing. The variable therefore represents broad economic composition. It does not directly measure the replacement of high-carbon manufacturing subsectors by low-carbon subsectors or the relocation of particular plants.
H2. Changes in the secondary-industry share form a statistical channel in the negative association between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions.

sec.title: 2.3. R&d expenditure and cleaner production
sec.p: Digital systems may support experimentation, simulation, and the acquisition of technical information. These capabilities make an R&D channel plausible, but expenditure is an input measure rather than evidence of successful environmental innovation. Research spending may support new products, expansion, or process improvements unrelated to energy use. Conversely, firms can adopt cleaner equipment developed elsewhere without a corresponding increase in local R&D expenditure.

The distinction matters when comparing manufacturing regions. Digital transformation and carbon competitiveness [13] concern a different outcome from expenditure-based mediation. Technological diversification and specialization [14] likewise describe innovation characteristics that an aggregate spending measure cannot capture. The hypothesis below is therefore evaluated using the stated proxy, and its interpretation remains specific to that proxy.
H3. R&D expenditure forms a statistical channel in the negative association between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions.

sec.title: 2.4. Decoupling and the energy requirements of digitalization
sec.p: Tapio’s framework [19] classifies the relationship between changes in emissions and economic activity. Strong decoupling means falling emissions alongside increasing output; weak decoupling allows emissions to rise more slowly than output. These states describe observed trajectories. Their occurrence does not identify which policy or technology produced them.

The digital sector itself has a carbon footprint. Reviews of ICT emissions [20] and evidence on data-centre energy use [21] show the importance of system boundaries, energy efficiency, and changing demand. An apparent improvement in a manufacturing fuel-combustion inventory may coexist with rising electricity use. The present decoupling analysis therefore complements the regression evidence but does not measure the complete environmental footprint of digital development.

Decoupling analysis is used as a descriptive complement to the regression results. It characterizes manufacturing output and emissions trajectories without estimating the contribution of digital economy development to individual decoupling transitions.

sec.title: 2.5. Recent evidence and regional contingencies
sec.p: Recent studies continue to broaden the empirical question. Research on fiscal decentralization and carbon intensity [22] examines institutional conditions; work on heterogeneous carbon-efficiency relationships [23] considers differences across settings; and city-level efficiency analysis [24] examines potential industrial and innovation pathways. Studies of urban emissions [25] and energy transition [26] further place digitalization within a changing energy system. These outcomes should not be treated as interchangeable with the absolute fuel-combustion emissions examined here.

Structural decomposition research [27] is especially relevant because changes in digital production and digital applications can have different upstream and downstream consequences. Evidence on industrial-structure mediation and spatial spillovers [28], spatial relationships across cities [29], and provincial spillover channels [30] motivates a model that allows cross-city dependence without imposing a predetermined spillover sign. Research on internet development and energy consumption [31] provides another reason to distinguish digital connectivity from energy savings.

The literature also connects digital development to green innovation [32], green total factor productivity [33], energy efficiency [34], and firm environmental performance [35]. These strands motivate the choice of mechanisms, but their measures and levels of aggregation differ from the present city panel. Provincial evidence on digital development, technological progress, and emissions [36] offers a closer comparator, although intensity can fall while absolute emissions increase. The contribution of the present study is consequently a focused regional comparison, not a claim that the digital economy–carbon relationship has not previously been studied.

sec.title: 2.6. Spatial relationships and the study framework
sec.p: Spatial econometrics distinguishes regression parameters from direct, indirect, and total impacts [37]. A city can respond to changes elsewhere through production linkages, shared infrastructure, and feedback. A significant spatial autoregressive parameter does not establish a significant spillover from digital development; that proposition requires the corresponding impact estimate and its uncertainty.

Firm-level research links digital technology and green innovation to manufacturing carbon performance [38]. At the regional scale, studies of interregional

Research on digitalization, IND, and green economic growth [41] also motivates the composition channel considered here. Together, these studies suggest that lower emissions recorded in one city need not imply an equivalent reduction across the regional production network.

H4. Digital economy development is associated with a non-zero cross-city spillover in manufacturing carbon emissions. The direction is left open because production relocation and cleaner-technology diffusion can imply different signs.

The core–periphery comparison is an additional exploratory analysis. A negative coefficient in one group and an insignificant coefficient in another do not by themselves establish a significant difference between groups. Likewise, observational mediation requires assumptions beyond those needed to estimate ordinary conditional associations [42], [43]. Research on digitalization and energy consumption [44] and interregional digital-economy linkages [45] reinforce the need to keep the proposed mechanisms, observed proxies, and accounting boundaries aligned. These distinctions guide the interpretation of the results below.

sec.title: 3.1. Study area and data sources
sec.p: This study examined nine cities in the PRD, namely Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Foshan, Huizhou, Dongguan, Zhongshan, Jiangmen, and Zhaoqing. These cities constitute the mainland manufacturing component of the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area. Hong Kong and Macao were excluded because their statistical systems, economic structures, and manufacturing profiles differ substantially from those of the nine mainland cities. Restricting the analysis to the PRD cities provided a more comparable regional setting for examining the relationship between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions.

The dataset covered the period from 2011 to 2024 and comprised 126 city–year observations. Data were compiled from the municipal statistical yearbooks and annual statistical communiqués of the nine cities (2012–2025 editions), the Guangdong Statistical Yearbook, provincial and municipal energy-intensity statistics, the Peking University Digital Financial Inclusion Index, and meteorological statistical records. Manufacturing energy consumption per unit of output and manufacturing output value were used to estimate carbon dioxide emissions, while economic, industrial, digital infrastructure, and innovation indicators were compiled from the corresponding statistical sources. Appendix A records the source and construction of each variable.

Missing observations were treated using linear interpolation within individual cities where adjacent observations were available. Where interpolation was not feasible, missing values were estimated using growth rates from comparable cities within Guangdong Province. The digital economy index for 2020 was taken from the linearly interpolated version of the source table because the original 2020 values contained a documented anomaly, and the 2024 values were recalculated as described in Section 3.2.2. Variables enter the regressions in constant 2011 prices and in logarithmic form where indicated. No winsorization was applied; the descriptive statistics in Section 3.7 therefore reflect the compiled series.
The resulting panel was used for the descriptive analysis, baseline regressions, spatial econometric estimation, and mechanism tests.

sec.title: 3.2.2 Digital economy development
sec.p: Digital economy development was measured using a composite index adapted from the city-level measurement framework discussed by Zhao et al. [47].

Five indicators were included, following the city-level framework of Zhao et al. [47]: the digital financial inclusion index, the internet penetration rate (internet users per 100 residents), the share of employment in information transmission, software, and information technology services, internet-related output per capita (telecommunications business volume per capita), and mobile internet users per 100 residents.

These indicators represented different dimensions of digital economy development. Digital financial inclusion, measured by the aggregate Peking University Digital Financial Inclusion Index, reflected access to financial services supported by digital technologies. The internet penetration rate and mobile internet subscriptions captured connectivity and individual adoption. The employment share of information technology services represented the supply of digital services and related human resources, while internet-related output per capita captured the economic scale of digital activity.

sec.title: 3.2.3 Mechanism and control variables
sec.p: Two variables were used to examine the potential mechanisms linking digital economy development to manufacturing carbon emissions.

IND was measured as the share of secondary-industry value added in regional gross domestic product, expressed as a percentage. This variable served as a proxy for broad industrial restructuring. It did not directly measure changes in the composition of manufacturing subsectors.
R&D expenditure (RD) was used to represent innovation inputs. The natural logarithm of R&D expenditure, denoted by ln RD, was employed in the econometric analysis.

The baseline models also included economic development, foreign direct investment, energy intensity, IND, R&D expenditure, and precipitation as control variables. Per capita GDP and foreign direct investment were expressed in logarithmic form. Energy intensity was measured using the percentage change in energy consumption per unit of output, while annual precipitation was included in logarithmic form.

IND and R&D expenditure were included as controls in the full baseline specifications and were examined separately as potential mediating variables in the mechanism analysis. The definitions and measurements of the study variables are presented in Table 2.

sec.p: A two-way fixed-effects model was first estimated to examine the association between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions without explicitly incorporating spatial interactions.
The baseline specification was:

The fixed-effects specification controls for unobserved city characteristics that remain constant over time and for shocks common to all cities in a given year. It does not, however, eliminate potential bias arising from time-varying omitted variables or reverse causality. The estimated coefficients were therefore interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects.

sec.title: 4.4. Spatial impact decomposition

sec.title: 5.1. Digital economy development and manufacturing decarbonization
sec.p: The empirical analysis revealed a negative relationship between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions in the baseline fixed-effects and spatial panel specifications. The coefficient remained negative and significant when an alternative spatial weight matrix was used and when the 2024 observations were excluded; under the carbon-intensity specification it was positive and statistically insignificant.

These findings were broadly consistent with previous research reporting negative associations between digital development and carbon emission performance in China [1], [2], [3], [5]. However, the present study also showed that the relationship varied across cities within a relatively integrated manufacturing region.

The distinction between the baseline SDM coefficient and the spatial impact estimates is important. Although the coefficient for digital economy development in the SDM was statistically significant, the estimated average direct effect and total effect were not statistically significant at conventional levels. Accordingly, the results provide evidence of a negative conditional relationship in the reported regression specifications, but the spatial impact decomposition does not establish a statistically significant average marginal effect.

This distinction matters for the interpretation of digitalization as a low-carbon development strategy. Digital technologies may support more efficient production, better resource allocation, and changes in industrial composition. At the same time, digital infrastructure requires additional energy, and improvements in productivity may stimulate manufacturing output. The environmental outcome therefore depends on how digital technologies interact with local industrial activities.

The findings suggest that digital development should not be treated as a uniform source of manufacturing emission reductions. Its association with carbon performance appears to depend on the structure and development stage of the regional manufacturing economy.

sec.title: 5.2. Industrial restructuring and the role of innovation
sec.p: The mediation analysis found a statistically significant indirect association involving the secondary-industry share. The estimated indirect association accounted for 29.82% of the total association in the non-spatial mediation model.

This result was consistent with the theoretical argument that changes in industrial composition can affect regional carbon performance. Digital connectivity may facilitate the reorganization of production networks and the expansion of higher-value economic activities. Such changes can alter the relative importance of manufacturing and service activities within local economies.

However, the IND variable measured the share of secondary-industry value added in regional GDP. It did not distinguish between cleaner and more emissions-intensive manufacturing subsectors. Consequently, the mediation result cannot establish whether the observed relationship arose from improvements within manufacturing, service-sector expansion, or changes in the geographical distribution of production.

The R&D channel presented a different pattern. The estimated indirect association was negative but statistically insignificant. This finding did not support R&D expenditure as a statistically detectable mediating variable in the present sample.

One possible explanation concerns the distinction between innovation inputs and technological outcomes. R&D expenditure measures the resources allocated to research activities, but it does not directly capture the adoption of energy-saving technologies or the environmental performance of innovation. Research expenditure may also accompany the expansion of industrial production, particularly in cities where manufacturing capacity and capital investment continue to grow.

The findings therefore point to the importance of distinguishing industrial restructuring from technological innovation when examining manufacturing decarbonization. They also suggest that future research should incorporate more direct indicators of green technological outcomes, including environmentally related patents, industrial energy efficiency, and the adoption of low-carbon production technologies.

sec.title: 5.3. Spatial dependence and regional differences
sec.p: The spatial analysis showed that manufacturing carbon emissions became more spatially clustered during the study period. The reported Moran’s I increased from 0.0130 in 2011 to 0.4647 in 2024, with statistically significant positive spatial autocorrelation in the later years.

This pattern indicated that cities with similar manufacturing emission levels became more geographically concentrated. However, spatial clustering alone does not identify the processes responsible for this pattern. Industrial relocation, differences in manufacturing specialization, common regional shocks, and changes in energy use may all contribute to spatial dependence.

The spatial impact decomposition did not identify a statistically significant indirect effect of digital economy development on manufacturing emissions. The estimated indirect effect was positive (0.2026) with a bootstrap standard error of 0.2982, and the corresponding total effect was $-$0.1320 with a standard error of 0.5234. Neither estimate differs from zero at conventional levels.

This finding provided no clear statistical support for either negative emission spillovers associated with cleaner technology diffusion or positive spillovers associated with emissions displacement. The absence of a statistically significant indirect effect should not be interpreted as evidence that cross-city production relationships are unimportant. Rather, such relationships were not detected through the estimated spatial impact measure.

The regional subgroup analysis further indicated differences between core and peripheral cities. The DE coefficient was negative and statistically significant in the pooled core-city subsample and positive but statistically insignificant in the peripheral-city subsample.

These differences may reflect variations in industrial specialization, digital infrastructure, and the types of production activities undertaken in different cities. The contrasting subgroup estimates are consistent with differences in industrial and digital development conditions across cities.

The available evidence does not establish that the differences were caused by the relocation of emissions-intensive production. Nevertheless, the findings support the need to examine manufacturing decarbonization at both city and regional levels, particularly where industrial supply chains cross administrative boundaries.

sec.title: 5.4. Policy implications
sec.p: The findings have several implications for digital development and low-carbon manufacturing policy in the PRD and other manufacturing-oriented urban regions.

First, because fuel-by-fuel physical consumption for the manufacturing sector is not published at the city level, the fuel-level sum in Eq. (1) was evaluated at the standard-coal aggregate with the raw-coal coefficient, so the procedure does not identify the fuel mix, and industrial process emissions such as those from cement and steel production are not separately counted. The series is measured in tonnes of

after the 44/12 conversion. Future research could incorporate fuel-specific combustion data, electricity-related emissions, and process emissions to provide a more complete assessment.

Second, industrial restructuring policies should consider carbon performance across the wider regional production network. Changes in the industrial composition of individual cities may reduce locally recorded emissions without producing equivalent reductions across the region. Policies supporting industrial relocation should therefore incorporate energy-efficiency requirements, emissions reporting, and cleaner production standards for receiving industrial parks and enterprises.

Third, innovation policies should distinguish between research expenditure and environmental outcomes. R&D expenditure measures innovation inputs rather than environmental outcomes. Innovation programmes could therefore be evaluated using measured energy and carbon outcomes alongside research expenditure. Evaluation systems could place greater weight on improvements in industrial energy efficiency, the adoption of cleaner production processes, and measurable reductions in emissions per unit of output.

Fourth, regional coordination remains important even where statistical spillover effects are not detected. Shared emissions-monitoring arrangements, consistent industrial carbon accounting standards, and cooperation between core-city technology providers and peripheral manufacturing enterprises may improve the evaluation of regional decarbonization efforts.

These policy considerations are relevant to other developing manufacturing regions where digital infrastructure is expanding alongside changes in industrial composition. The central implication is that digital development and low-carbon manufacturing policy should be coordinated with IND, technological capacity, and the geographical organization of production.

sec.title: 5.5. Limitations and future research
sec.p: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.

First, manufacturing carbon emissions were estimated from the direct combustion of eight energy sources. The inventory did not include indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity or process-related emissions from industries such as cement and steel. These accounting boundaries may affect comparisons among cities with different energy systems and INDs. Future research could incorporate electricity-related emissions, industrial process emissions, and supply-chain carbon accounting to provide a more complete assessment of regional manufacturing carbon performance.

Second, the IND variable represented the share of secondary-industry value added in regional GDP. Although suitable for describing broad changes in economic composition, it did not directly measure restructuring within manufacturing. More detailed information on manufacturing subsectors, production relocation, and sector-specific carbon intensity would allow the industrial restructuring mechanism to be examined more precisely.

Third, R&D expenditure was an input-based indicator of innovation. It did not capture the direction, adoption, or environmental performance of technological change. Future studies could use green patent indicators, industrial energy-saving technology adoption, and firm-level innovation outcomes to distinguish general innovation activity from innovation directly related to manufacturing decarbonization.

Fourth, the digital economy index was constructed using annually calculated entropy weights. This approach captured differences in the annual distribution of digital indicators but limited strict comparisons of index levels across years. A composite index based on common normalization parameters and fixed weights would provide a useful alternative for examining longitudinal relationships.

Finally, the empirical models identified conditional associations rather than causal effects. City and year fixed effects accounted for time-invariant city characteristics and common temporal shocks, but time-varying confounding factors and reverse causality remained possible. Future studies could examine suitable policy interventions, externally driven infrastructure changes, or credible instrumental-variable strategies to strengthen causal identification.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study examined the relationship between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon emissions in nine PRD cities from 2011 to 2024. Using fixed-effects and spatial econometric models, mediation analysis, decoupling measures, and regional subgroup regressions, the study investigated the overall association, potential mechanisms, spatial dependence, and differences between core and peripheral cities.

In the non-spatial mediation model, the indirect association involving the secondary-industry share represented 29.82% of the estimated total association. The corresponding indirect association involving R&D expenditure was not statistically significant. The spatial indirect effect was also statistically insignificant, providing no clear evidence of a measurable cross-city emission response associated with digital economy development.

The subgroup regressions showed different coefficient patterns across the two groups. The digital economy coefficient was negative and statistically significant in the four core cities but positive and insignificant in the five peripheral cities. These findings suggest that the relationship between digital development and manufacturing emissions varies with regional industrial conditions rather than following a uniform pattern.

The study contributes evidence on the roles of industrial composition and regional heterogeneity in the relationship between digital economy development and manufacturing carbon performance. For manufacturing-intensive urban regions, the findings support differentiated digital development strategies, closer integration of industrial and carbon policies, and regional accounting arrangements that distinguish genuine emissions reductions from changes in the location of production.
